historical_references.reference: Timon of Athens was a character in a play by William Shakespeare, first performed around 1608. In the play, Timon is a generous but disillusioned nobleman who gives away his wealth to those he believes are his friends, only to be betrayed and abandoned once his money is gone. There is no clear historical basis for this character, but the name Timon may have been inspired by the ancient Greek philosopher and misanthrope Timon of Phlius, who lived around 320 BC and is known for his bitterness and rejection of human society.

historical_references.reference: The ancient Greek philosopher and misanthrope Timon of Phlius lived around 320 BC. He was a contemporary of Aristotle and is known for his extreme bitterness and rejection of human society. Timon is often depicted as living in a cave and abandoning his wife, Megara, and son, Timas, in order to live a solitary life.
